props.title: Snake Eyes
props.initialSlug: Fate's deadliest roll of the dice.

sections.content: Brian De Palma's Snake Eyes exemplifies the director's virtuosic camera work and Hitchcockian suspense, opening with an astounding 13-minute continuous shot that follows Nicolas Cage's corrupt detective through a boxing match and casino. This technical achievement recalls De Palma's earlier tracking shots in Carlito's Way (1993) and builds on the tradition of complex long takes like those in Touch of Evil (1958). The film's conspiracy thriller elements and unreliable perspective connect it to De Palma's other paranoid masterworks like Blow Out (1981) and Body Double (1984).

sections.content: The late 1990s saw a resurgence of complex conspiracy thrillers, with Snake Eyes joining films like Enemy of the State (1998) and The Game (1997) in exploring paranoia through cutting-edge filmmaking techniques. De Palma's use of split-screen and multiple perspectives to show conflicting versions of events builds on techniques he pioneered in Sisters (1972) and Dressed to Kill (1980), while anticipating later unreliable narrator films like Memento (2000).

The film's Atlantic City setting provides a neon-drenched backdrop that De Palma uses to full effect, creating a morally ambiguous playground similar to his Chicago sequences in The Untouchables (1987). Nicolas Cage's over-the-top performance as Detective Rick Santoro fits perfectly within De Palma's operatic style, recalling other theatrical performances in his films like John Lithgow in Raising Cain (1992). sections.content: The film's ambitious opening sequence represents a technical milestone in steadicam operation, rivaling other famous long takes like those in Goodfellas (1990) and Touch of Evil (1958). De Palma's integration of CGI to achieve impossible camera moves pointed toward future innovations in films like Birdman (2014), while maintaining his characteristic split-screen techniques and voyeuristic themes.
